title: Mike Todasco: From Comic Books to Corporate Innovation to AI Education

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Hello, welcome back to the Starting Story podcast with me, Krishna Parmar. Here I interview entrepreneurs and business leaders around the world to find out more about how they started and the story that's taken them to where they are today. Today's guest is Michael Todasco, or just Mike. He has a background that started in finance and accounting, and then he transitioned into the tech industry. His entrepreneurial journey first started with founding an e-commerce company called Sketch Maven, which, even though it failed, provided him with, I'm sure, loads of learning experiences. He later joined PayPal, where he led the innovation group, focusing on projects like the Global Innovation Tournaments.

Currently, he's deeply engaged in AI. He advises companies and teaches at San Diego State University in America. He's exploring how AI can enhance personal empowerment and has over 100 US patents in various different fields, not just AI. He values authenticity and enjoys sharing his experiences to inspire others. Hopefully, this should be a very interesting and insightful conversation between me and Michael, and I look forward to finding out more about how he started and his story so far. Join me as we talk to Michael Todasco about his starting story. Mike, thank you so much for coming onto the Starting Story podcast with me today. It means a lot.

You're a very special guest with so much you've done. Like I was saying in the intro, you've gone all the way from kind of finance to tech. You're also delving in this modern frontier of AI. Really kind of a thorough resume behind your name. Do you want to talk a little bit more about who you are and what you do and what kind of interests you?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Yeah. First, thanks for having me. I'm glad to be here. I'm excited for a fun conversation with you today, and hopefully we can help or inspire a few people as part of it. My background, look, first and foremost, I'm a parent. I got two kids, 11 and 13. They are the focus of all things I do. I have an amazing wife that I've been married to for over 20 years. And beyond that, I am a son, and all these things, my parents are still with us, God willing. And I, you know, also dabble in a lot of business stuff. I've always been into business ever since I was a little kid, selling baseball cards and comic books, paying my way through college by doing that.
I've always been fascinated with the world of business and finance, and that is just something that has kind of carried through throughout my life and throughout my career. So that's me.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Okay, nice. So, I didn't realize that's how early you started, all the way back in college. It's one of those things where you don't really think of it as being an entrepreneur, do you, when you're selling baseball stuff? You don't go, "Oh, I'm a big entrepreneur." It's just about making a small buck. But how come you are interested in business from such a young age? Is there any experience behind it? What kind of first got that twinkle where you were like, "Hmm, I kind of like making this money"? Honestly, Krishna,

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: I don't know fully. I think maybe my mom at least was really cheap, and money was very much a focus always, and so there was always an interest in that. And I remember I was six years old actually, and my parents got me my first, my dad purchased my first baseball cards for me. And for folks outside of the US, trading cards, things like that, like Pokémon cards, but these are for baseball players, especially back in the 1980s when I was growing up, that was the big thing, the big sport for this. And I didn't, no, I did like baseball. I never really played baseball, but at some point soon after that, I would collect them, and at some point I got a price guide.

And that was this real unlock to see numbers go up, numbers go down, and that these little pieces of cardboard had value to other people. I didn't know this was right in the middle of a collectibles boom in the 1980s. I didn't know that, so the numbers largely were going up, so it was a very exciting time, and I just kind of got into that. And you know, I collected as a kid, I traded with friends. By the age of 12, I was selling to actual dealers, walking into stores and selling stuff. By the age of 14, I was working in a store myself, like I got hired to work in one.

And then at like 16 or so, I was doing conventions. And then when I went off to school, would have been 1995, I actually started like a mail order catalog because it was too hard to do conventions and stuff. And eventually I started selling stuff online. Most people are like, "Yeah, you started selling on eBay." No, no, no, this was before eBay. This was on Yahoo Auctions, which people don't even realize was a thing. It was actually really great for a couple of years to sell stuff, and then eBay kind of took over everything. But yeah, so I did that all through college. I got to be pretty good at it.
I mean, I was obsessed with it. And anything you're obsessed with in life is almost by definition something that if you really apply yourself, you will be good at. So I got to be pretty good.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Yeah, wow. Well, that's true right there. You have to do what you're already interested in, right? Otherwise, it feels like a chore trying to do that work. So,

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Yeah. And Krishna, to that point, I would sometimes, especially when I'd come back from college, I'd be up until like 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning working on stuff, organizing, building a catalog, and it never felt like work or anything to me. I just enjoyed doing it. That's exactly right.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Amazing. Well, okay, that's eye-opening. I didn't realize that's how early your journey started. So then you went into college. What were you studying at college?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: I went to college as a finance major. That's how I entered, mostly because finance was related to money in some way, and so I figured, "Oh, well, that sort of makes sense." I kind of explored a bunch of things. I went to University of Illinois, so engineering was a big thing. Maybe I dabbled in that for a few weeks. My mom was an actuary, so I took like an actuarial science class, and none of that. And I wound up graduating a finance major, even though I kind of had all these parallel paths. I even worked in an advertising agency while I was in college and stuff like that as well. But I started in finance, I ended in

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Finance. Okay, I mean, natural progression. If you're interested in business and money, then at that time, finance is like the next step, isn't it? You're not going to enter engineering, are you? So, makes sense. And then after finance, you then pursued an actual finance career, right? You went into working. Yeah,

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: So in finance, there's a few different paths that you could take out of college typically. There's investments, kind of the personal finance side. There's investment banking, which would be mergers, acquisitions, stuff like that. Most people, I'd say probably the biggest one is corporate finance, and that's the world that I entered. And the company that I worked for was GE, General Electric, which back in 1999 when I graduated, was the most valuable company in the world. And it's almost funny to think nowadays, like "Wow, GE?" No, it was the undisputed champ. Jack Welch, who was the CEO at the time, I mean, I took a management class, and the teacher talked about Jack Welch at length.

He was, I think, Fortune actually said he was the manager of the century. That's what they called him. And then GE fell apart after he left. And that's a whole another thing about maybe he wasn't quite as brilliant as everyone thought. Sorry, go ahead, Krishna. Yeah,

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Yeah. So, I mean, that's interesting. You go into this finance career, right? And on the side, because you'd already started this business, in retrospect, you think about it with the whole cards, right? Did you keep that going during college and even after college, or did that kind of take a sideline?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: It's funny. So, at some point, very soon after college, I got a girlfriend, became my wife. It was one of those things like, "I'm an adult now. I don't need to be doing this anymore." But that said, got married, a few years later was going back to school to get my MBA and thinking about ideas, and I always kept idea files. And that was actually the job I did after my MBA, was getting back into that and creating my own comic book related business in fact. So, it's funny. I completely went away from it, almost kind of disowned it as a hobby, and within five, six years after that, was right back into

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: It again. Amazing. Because that's the thing, right? With lots of people that do start businesses early on, just because you have so much spare time when you're a child or even when you're a teen, as soon as you start working after college, all that spare time is eaten up by either work or the exhaustion after work. So, you kind of eventually fall away from it. So, it's nice to hear that you picked it back up again, almost naturally realizing that this is still valuable, this is still something I want to do. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: And one pro tip I will give for people out there, and this is just, I just wish everybody would do this: when you have ideas, when you have inspiration in life, write those things down somewhere because you never know when it's going to be useful. So, put it in your iPhone, use Google Keep, Evernote. Back in the day, I used to literally keep a file folder of just pieces of paper that I would drop in there. And that was part of the inspiration. Sometimes like years later, I would go back in and literally the idea that I built the business off of, which became known as Sketch Maven, came from one of those ideas I probably had five, six years before that.

So, pro tip for everybody: ideas are so valuable, especially in the age we're entering now of AI and so forth. Keep those. Don't think it's bad, good, it doesn't matter. Just all your ideas, just keep somewhere.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Yeah, I agree. Because think about to-do lists, right? To-do lists are obviously not for ideas, they're for tasks, but the rhetoric is the same. The whole point of a to-do list is you'll forget the tasks, so write it down somewhere. So, it's the same thing for an idea, right? There's so many times I've had an idea, literally going to bed, and I'd be like, "You know what? I'll write this on the next day." And you wake up the next day and you're like, "God damn it, I forgot what that idea was." You're like, "I can't believe I've forgotten it. I should have just got up and written it down." So, it's one of those, it's like a to-do list but for ideas, and you can keep it there, except there's no time frame behind it. Whenever you feel the need for inspiration, you can just delve back into it and pick something up, right?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: 100%. So, to that, pro tip number two I'll give people: go onto Amazon, go to whatever, go to your local stationary store, buy like a bulk thing of notepads and put them in every room in your house. Have one, and buy pens too, and have them in every dresser, have them everywhere. Throw one into your car. It doesn't matter. Yes, you always have your phone by you, but look, in the middle of the night, I don't sleep with my phone. My phone stays very far away from me when I'm going to bed, but I have a notepad. So, if I do wake up at 3:00 in the morning, I just jot something down, and then it's out of my mind. I don't need to worry about it, and I go back to sleep.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Exactly. Well, talking about ideas, you said about Sketch Maven, right, which was your e-commerce store. So, you said that it failed. It didn't do what you expected. It failed miserably. Okay. So, explain a bit more. What was your ideation behind getting it started? What were your plans for it initially? Yeah.

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: So, here was the inspiration. It would have actually started probably when I was in college. The inspiration comes from comic books, and that from every comic book, it came from a hand-drawn piece of artwork. So, literally, if you've read a Spider-Man comic before, there was an artist who actually drew that picture back in the day. Now it's on tablets. Back in the day, they drew this on actual pieces of paper, and that is the original artwork behind it. And so, it's a very unique problem where there are millions of pages out there in the world that millions of people have seen, but there is only one copy, original copy of each and every one of those millions of pages.

And it started because there was a comic book cover, it was for a comic called Green Lantern, that I really, I saw at a convention when I was a kid. The artist was there. It was like $150. I didn't have that kind of money. And at some point later on, I was like, "eBay was out there and all this." This was the early 2000s, years later. I'm like, "Oh, I'm going to go buy that." And that's when I realized, if you're trying to find something where there's only one of it in the world, it is a really, really hard thing to do. There's only one Mona Lisa, but there's enough documentation to know, "Okay, it's in the Louvre." You go to Paris, that is how you find it.

You know how to do it. But for everything else, the millions of comic book pages, who knows where these things are? We don't even know if they exist anymore. So, it was a marketplace built around that. The bigger theory was that in 2009 when I started this, collectibles were underserved by sites like eBay. And that if you wanted to buy sneakers and you were a sneakerhead, it wasn't really structured for that. Yeah, there are a lot of people on there, but eBay was a one-size-fits-all model. And that you can build all of these niche collectibles marketplaces, tailor-focused to serve a community, and that would serve it better.

And Comic Art was one that was small, but it was manageable, and it was like, "Okay, this is a good place for me to start this hypothesis." And this was before Goat and StockX and all of these other things came to serve that same niche. So, I built it. I had no idea what I was doing. I was hiring designers off of Upwork and developers to build this. I remember, Krishna, when we launched it, I did not even, day one it launches, and I'm testing checkout, and I'm like, "Oh, it's not even a secure checkout." People are putting their credit card number, and there's not even the little lock up there.

I didn't put that in the specs. And this was before Stripe or anything like that. So, all of these were problems. I'm like, "Oh my God, I need to fix that, I need to fix this." It was hard for a non-developer who had never done a website before to do that.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: I can imagine. Yeah, go ahead. I can imagine. I mean, now you've got Shopify for e-commerce, and even if you try to make a basic website now, you can do all non-code, right? You can just drag and drop blocks. Obviously, back then, you need to get a developer in who'd do everything. Even as you said yourself, for secure checkout, you have Stripe nowadays, all this stuff. Whereas back then, you had to manually code all that, which is just so much effort for someone who hasn't touched a line of code ever, right?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Yeah, I mean, and I learned some PHP. I was able to do a few things here or there, but the site was getting hacked and all that. The best piece of advice came from my sister-in-law, who's an academic, who we were with her one Christmas. She was like, "Hey, how's the business going?" I'm like, "I'm not well. It just started to get hacked, people are taking data, and all this other kind of stuff." And she said to me very innocently, she was like, "Well, I guess that means your site's doing well enough to get hacked." And I'm like, "I guess you're right there." It wasn't hacked day one.

You do need some sort of traction to actually have hackers trying to get into your site, and it was quite easy for them to do that. But so, this was just all stuff for me to learn. And look, I learned more in those two years of building and running that site than at any other time, any other two-year span of my career. It was amazing. I say it was a failure just because in the end, it didn't get to where I wanted to be. There are a lot of little successes I had in there, but in the end, after two years, I just had to make the hard decision of, "Okay, I'm not going to do this anymore. I need to move on to something else."

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Okay. So, when you initially said it was a complete failure, I thought it was just kind of like you put loads of effort into it but it went nowhere. But it seems like it was still making sales, you were still kind of attracting some people. It was more just the logistics of running or maintaining the site that seemed to just take over the actual benefits of keeping it going, right?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Yeah, I mean, there were sales, but every month, Krishna, there was more money going out than there was coming in, and that's only sustainable for so long. So, there were some sales, there were some things, but even just storing images was much more expensive, much harder to do back in 2010 than it was today. So, even just my AWS costs were fairly high at that time. So, all of these things, it just did not get where I wanted to do because the ultimate vision wasn't just comic art, it was shoes and collectible pens and watches or whatever else. It was all these other things and just never got to that point. Yeah,

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: I think the only thing that kind of stopped you maybe at that time was just, I don't know, maybe just the lack of funds to hire an excellent developer maybe who could just seal the gaps. And there were just too many gaps that sand was just running through them, and it was hard to patch them up.

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: So, one of the things, I was living in Silicon Valley at the time. I was actually going to school at Berkeley, which is part of one of the schools up here in the valley. So, I was talking to a lot of people who were founders, and the one piece of feedback I was getting again and again and again was, "You need to find a technical co-founder." I did hear that time and time again. I talked to several different people about being that technical co-founder to help out with all of that. But I think honestly, I was looking and asking for too much from them because not only I wanted them to be technical, I wanted them to love comic books as much as me and understand the business side.

I was looking for a clone of me plus all the tech stuff, when in reality I should have just been like, "Clone of me and just a rough interest in some of the things." I was being way too stringent, and that's why at some point I was like, "Well, I'm just going to go off and do this on my own." And honestly, it was lonely too. When you're the only person, when you're hiring a bunch of people from India and other places that are on the other side of the world, it's tough. It was tough doing that. And if I had that technical co-founder, we could have at least been supportive of each other as part of

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: That. Yeah, no, that's true. That kind of loneliness with entrepreneurship is so true. And having a co-founder, or even if you don't have a co-founder, having a group of people who understand you and what you're trying to do can make such a big difference, right? So, once you left Sketch Maven, you realized this is done for, I'm going to move on, do something different. What was that something different that you moved

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: Onto? The criteria for finding a job was it had to make money. That was basically as far as my criteria went. Luckily, I was living in Silicon Valley at the time. And part of it also was I had my first kid. It was one of those things like I was doing some side consulting to pay some bills and all that, but it was completely unrelated to Sketch Maven. But that made me travel, which is harder being away from the kid and all that. I'm like, "I just need something local and stable." I remember there were two companies I interviewed with that gave me offers. One was IAC, which had a business called Ask.com.

And so, this was like one of the old-school search engines, like Ask Jeeves, like 2011. It was still around. I had an offer from there. It was up in Oakland, a little bit of a drive. But then something closer was PayPal, which was actually right down the street from me. I had used PayPal for credit card processing. I had signed up for PayPal back in 99 or 2000 when they were bribing people by giving you 10 or 20 bucks to sign up for the service. So, I'd used it for a long time, and I had a lot of friends from school that were there. That's how I originally got introduced.

And got offers from both. It wasn't hard to make that call to join PayPal, especially because I thought they were kind of crazy for hiring me because I didn't feel I was qualified at all. I wasn't qualified. And I'm like, "Why are they hiring me here?" But I'm like, "I'm going with it, I'm going with it."

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: So, you went into PayPal and you did some, like what specific department? It sounds like you were pointing to some side department, what was it called? It was called the Global Innovation Tournaments. That sounds like something I've never heard before.

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: That was a little bit later on. So, initially I just joined the mobile team. That's back when mobile was separate from the rest of the company. This was 2011. David Marcus, who was at Facebook also, now very much an entrepreneur doing things in the crypto Bitcoin space, his company was bought and they kind of took over mobile. So, it was very entrepreneurial, like doing a lot of new and exciting things, kind of different than the rest of the culture at PayPal. And so, I actually came in as data analytics. It would later be called a data scientist, but that term wasn't really widely used in 2011.

And that's what I initially came in to do. So, I was doing that and product jobs for probably my first four or five years, like product manager, product marketing, all this, just jumping around, as I always like to say, being dangerously unqualified for every single job that I had there. But it was fun, and I was just constantly put into new challenges. And then when PayPal split from eBay, 2015 going into 2016, one of the opportunities we had was to create corporate functions, and that's when the opportunity to kind of like define what innovation was going to mean for our company and to kind of build that out, what that was going to look like. And so, that was the opportunity that I had, which frankly took me to my end of my career at PayPal.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Okay. Because that kind of is a bridge to what you're doing right now, isn't it? In terms of, if you're working with innovations, now you're working with AI and trying to delve deeper into it, which is obviously one of the biggest innovations in the last decade. So, kind of how, when was the first time you kind of had that exposure to AI? Was it when everyone else did, or because you were already working in a tech company, did you have it a little bit prior to when the rest of the world boomed? Oh,

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: At PayPal, we used a lot of AI and machine learning, so I was constantly being exposed to it. We never called it artificial intelligence. That was one of the things I learned back in the 2010s because we were coming out of an AI winter. For folks who don't know, ever since the 1950s, there's been all this hype about AI and the promise that it has, and then all of a sudden it doesn't do that, and then there's like what's known as AI winters. And really, we were coming out of another one of those in the 2010s, so it was all machine learning, deep learning. We talked a little bit about neural networks and things like that, but we never ever muttered the words AI, which was just funny how that panned out.

So, at that time though, like PayPal was really, really, I would say, using a lot of different methods and techniques out of necessity. And when I say that, what I mean is it was two specific areas in the company. It was risk and security because if you think about a company like PayPal, all that it's doing is, "You have money, you have money, we'll send the money between those two people." That's not a very hard problem. The hard part of the problem is, "Is this person who they claim to be? Is this person who they claim to be?" That is the hardest part. It's the identity part, which is the most difficult part in a two-sided transaction like that.

In person, it's cash, it doesn't matter, whatever it is. But when you're doing things electronically, that becomes a lot more difficult. And when you have billions and billions of transactions going across your platform, you can't do this through traditional coding, and you've got to be a step or two ahead of the bad guys. And that's why for years at PayPal, there were machine learning techniques to analyze transactions, to analyze accounts, and so forth. To do that, it was a necessity in the business. And so, like within that world of risk and security, we were world-class. In other parts of the business, especially when I was there, not so much in the AI world.

It was like you would think everything had it. No, for like marketing or something, we weren't using those tools for the most part in my time that was there. We would dabble, there would occasionally be a machine learning team in customer service. It never got the traction everyone was hoping for and some other things like that. But yeah, so I was exposed to it a lot in my time there, and also just in the world of innovation, I got to see a lot of the cool stuff either that we were building or other teams in the company were building.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Mm, so kind of what you've said so far, it sounds a lot like you're someone who's just like naturally curious about just how things work. Because I feel like when someone says they're, you know, dangerously underqualified for a job, then I'm thinking the only reason you kind of got in or the only reason you got in but still survived was because you were so curious that you would quickly pick up stuff and kind of integrate yourself. Because there are some people on the contrary who would be dangerously underqualified, go into the work, be recognized as dangerously underqualified, and get fired from the job. Yet you obviously weren't.

So clearly you're to pick up things quickly, right? And not only that, as we've seen in the corporate side and also in terms of business and then also in terms of AI, which is so new, but you're still kind of trying to be like on top of it, which is so difficult because every week I reckon there's like a new 100 chatbots that come out every single week. It's too hard to stay on top of it. What would you say to that?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: I say there's probably half right. Yes, yeah. I mean, look, I think for this to work and for frankly for anybody as we're entering this real age of AI that we're in right now, like you need to be curious. You need to be like you need to be experimenting with stuff. You need to know that hey, failure is just part of the process and just kind of put yourself out there and try things and not everything is going to work as part of that. And you know, those are things I try to instill at the company and I try to do myself. I wasn't always successful even in doing it myself.

Like some I mean, we're all we have pride, we have ego, we have all these other things. So it's sometimes hard to say like hey, I failed at this. It's not always the easiest thing in the in the world to do. Different types of failure as well to look at. So like I think that is really important for people as we enter this next age to really dive into that and just try these things out. And you've got to be curious about this. Like if it if you talk to a language model and the language model doesn't give you what you want, ask why. Either ask why in your own brain like oh maybe I didn't ask right.

Maybe I should have said this and this. Ask why it's in the model itself. Like these you know, large language models in the chat format that they're built in are so conversational. Like these need to be back and forth. You can't just go into it expecting for it to lead your mind. You got to just wonder why. You got to anticipate what how it's thinking and so forth. And like a lot of that is like if you anticipate how it's thinking, you got to be curious like well why does it think that way? And you know, ultimately just ask a lot of questions. But yes, like curiosity is going to be a superpower for everyone going forward, I think.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
paragraphs: Yeah, I agree because curiosity is has always been something a good skill to have rather than just being complacent and sitting where you are. But I think with this kind of new age and with just the amount of information that gets thrown out now with AI, it's like everything's gone into turmoil. Everything's gone complex and you know these like you said, large language models, they can be used in so many ways as well. Like I use them sometimes when I'm struggling on an Excel sheet and I'm struggling to find a particular formula. Before, I remember even before I'd have to go onto the actual Excel website, whatever thousand of pages they have, and try to figure out which actual flipping formula do I use.

Whereas now I can just go into the LLM and ask it please can you help me with this one? It'll give me the answer. And then all these little things even I know some people say they use it for emotional support, some people use it for like business guidance. It's like anything you can think of, you it's it's quite at least something that can help you out, right?

turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: So Oh, absolutely. And that's one thing for people who are you know, little hesitant to use these models, if there is anybody hopefully everybody watching this is not, but like if you are, think about an area in your life where there is opportunity. Like for me, you know, I give the example of my mother about a year ago gave me a call and she's like hey, I got to I'm going to the hospital. And the other thing we did was like we made it our patient advocates. We would say okay, given what you've seen here, what questions should we ask the doctor? Like what are important things that we should ask?

Like make us more informed for that. And honestly, Krishna, that made such a better experience. So my parents who were like never ever like we should use AI, found really quickly oh my god, you could use it for that. Well, here comes the curiosity. Well, what else could I use it for in my life? And that's what I always tell people like just start with something like cooking meals, like planning your travel, whatever it might be, wherever there's a pain point, wherever there's something you're passionate about, use it for that. Just spend some time with it and then you're going to see all these other applications where you can use that in your life to even help you even more so.

turns.speaker: Krishna Parmar
